questions.question: In the CBR-RAG legal casebase, how many unique legal acts were identified and how many cases had no reference to legal acts?
questions.expected_answer: 785 unique legal acts were identified, and 1,183 cases (57%) had no reference to legal acts (only 44 acts appeared in more than 1 case).
questions.evidence_quote: The most frequently mentioned act is the ‘Federal Court Rules’ out of 785 unique legal acts. Within the dataset, 1,183 (57%) cases were found to have no reference to legal acts, while only 44 acts appeared in more than 1 case.
required_evidence_clauses: 1,183 (57%) cases were found to have no reference to legal acts

questions.question: How do intra-embeddings f(.) and inter-embeddings g(.) differ in what they compare inside CBR-RAG?
questions.expected_answer: Intra-embeddings f(.) compare items of the same attribute type (such as questions to questions for semantic textual similarity), whereas inter-embeddings g(.) allow matching across different attribute types (such as a query to supporting text or entities).
questions.evidence_quote:
Intra Embeddings, f (·), optimised for attribute matching. These embeddings facilitate attribute-to-attribute comparisons where local similarities can be computed between the same types of attributes (e.g., questions with questions).

– Inter Embeddings, g(·), designed for information retrieval (IR) scenarios. These embeddings allow for matching that is not restricted to like attributes, enabling inter-attribute similarity assessment.
required_evidence_clauses: Intra Embeddings, f (·), optimised for attribute matching
Inter Embeddings, g(·), designed for information retrieval

questions.question: Why does AnglEBERT require a supervised paired training dataset unlike standard BERT?
questions.expected_answer: Because AnglE uses a contrastive learning strategy that needs positive and negative paired instances, whereas BERT can be trained unsupervised with MLM and NSP.
questions.evidence_quote: One of the difficulties when using AnglEBERT for a specific domain is that one must generate a supervised training set (unlike with BERT which can be trained in an unsupervised manner using the MLM and NSP self-supervision methods). This is because the AnglE method adopts a contrastive learning strategy, where the supervised dataset must include paired instances for training.

questions.question: In the evaluation section, how many ALQA cases remained in the CBR-RAG case-base after filtering offensive triplets?
questions.expected_answer: 2,084 cases remained after removing 40 offensive triplets from the original 2,124 triplets.

questions.question: Which hybrid algorithm, neighbor count k, and context option yielded the best cosine similarity score in CBR-RAG legal generation?
questions.expected_answer: Hybrid AnglEBERT with k = 3 using Full Case context achieved the highest score (0.9141, 1.94% higher on average than No-RAG).
questions.evidence_quote: The best semantic similarity was noted with the Hybrid AnglEBERT variant when 3 nearest neighbours were fed into the generator in the form of full cases forming context for RAG. It provided answers on average with 1.94% increase in performance.

questions.question: In RAGentA's hybrid retrieval stage, which dense embedding model, vector store, and alpha weight are used?
questions.expected_answer: intfloat/e5-base-v2 (E5) with Pinecone as vector store, fused with BM25 using alpha = 0.35.
questions.evidence_quote:
Our semantic retrieval is powered by dense embeddings using the intfloat/e5-base-v2 model (E5) with Pinecone as the vector store to capture nuanced semantic relationships [23].

These two systems are fused using a tunable interpolation parameter α∈[ 0, 1], producing a final document score as: Shybrid(d) = α· Ssparse(d)+( 1− α)· Sdense(d) (1) We set α = 0.35 to give slightly higher weight to dense retrieval while maintaining meaningful contribution from sparse retrieval.

questions.question: How does Agent-2 (Judge) in RAGentA filter retrieved documents using the dynamic threshold adjusted_tau_q?
questions.expected_answer: It computes adjusted_tau_q = tau_q - n * sigma with n = 0.5, keeps documents where score >= adjusted_tau_q, and filters out documents where score < adjusted_tau_q.
questions.evidence_quote: After scoring all documents, the system computes the mean score (τq) and standard deviation (σ), establishing a dynamic threshold as adjusted_τq = τq− n· σ, where n is a hyperparameter controlling filtering stringency. According to empirical analyses from the MAIN-RAG study, optimal performance is achieved at n = 0.5. Utilizing this dynamic threshold, the system retains documents where score≥ adjusted_τq and filters those where score < adjusted_τq.

questions.question: When Agent-4 (Reviser) detects answer gaps and runs follow-up retrieval in RAGentA, which documents are excluded?
questions.expected_answer: Previously retrieved documents are excluded from the follow-up retrieval pass to obtain complementary information.
questions.evidence_quote: When gaps are identified, Agent-4 initiates a targeted follow-up process: it generates questions to address these gaps and uses the hybrid retrieval system from initial phase, excluding previously retrieved documents to ensure complementary information.

questions.question: In the 2025 evaluation section, which open model replaced Claude-3.5 Sonnet as the automated evaluator in RAGentA and what score ranges were assigned?
questions.expected_answer: Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct acted as LLM-as-a-judge, assigning correctness in [-1, 2] and faithfulness in [-1, 1].
questions.evidence_quote: Instead of the closed-source Claude-3.5 Sonnet model, we use Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct as an LLM-as-a-judge, which receives the predicted answer, the ground-truth answer, and the cited passages. The LLM-as-a-judge assigns a correctness score in the range[−1, 2] and a faithfulness score in the range[−1, 1].

questions.evidence_quote: DBSCAN clustering algorithm might not always differentiate headers, footers and the main content, especially in highly variable PDF document formats. This misidentification could lead to loss of essential information in the further processing.

questions.question: What four robustness capabilities does the Retrieval-Augmented Generation Benchmark (RGB) test?
questions.expected_answer: Noise robustness, information integration, negative rejection, and counterfactual robustness.
questions.evidence_quote: In this work, we use the RGB corpus to evaluate LLMs in four scenarios: (1) noise robustness; (2) information integration; (3) negative rejection; and (4) counterfactual robustness.

questions.question: In the 2026 study evaluating GraphRAG robustness, what entity confidence cutoff, Leiden resolution value, and retrieved document count were fixed across experiments?
questions.expected_answer: Entity confidence threshold 0.7, Leiden resolution parameter 1.0, and 5 retrieved documents.
questions.evidence_quote: For the knowledge graph construction, a confidence score of 0.7 for entities was adopted which refers to the minimum threshold required for an entity to be included in the knowledge graph. The Leiden algorithm for community detection was used with a resolution parameter of 1.0. We kept the number of retrieved documents fixed to 5 for all experiments.

questions.question: In the noise robustness experiments with GPT-4o-mini, under which noise condition did GraphRAG outperform the RGB baseline?
questions.expected_answer: Only at the lowest noise ratio of 0.2.
questions.evidence_quote: For the GPT-4o-mini, GraphRAG achieved better results only for the lowest noise ratio of 0.2.
required_evidence_clauses: only for the lowest noise ratio of 0.2

questions.question: In the 2026 evaluation results for counterfactual robustness, how did GRcomb compare against the RGB baseline on GPT-4o-mini accuracy with counterfactual documents (ACC_doc) versus error detection (ED)?
questions.expected_answer: GRcomb reduced GPT-4o-mini ACC_doc to 35.35% versus 71% for RGB, but raised error detection (ED) to 100% versus 77% for RGB.
questions.evidence_quote: For the GPT-4o-mini, the same configuration had a negative impact on the results compared to the accuracy achieved with the RGB baseline, 71 %, although it outperformed all other GraphRAG configuration, achieving 35.35 %. On the other hand, in terms of error detection (ED), the combination of the LLM encoded knowledge and external knowledge, GRcomb, led to the best results, achieving 94.94 % and 100 %, respectively, for GPT-3.5 and GPT-4o-mini, while the RGB benchmark achieved 7 % and 77 %.

questions.question: In the negative rejection experiments, why did GRdef obtain the lowest rejection rate for GPT-4o-mini (12.66%), and what overall limitation remained across all tested configurations?
questions.expected_answer: GRdef reveals the model's propensity to be overconfident in its encoded knowledge; overall, every configuration had rejection rates below 50%, showing RAG systems still struggle to reject unanswerable queries.
questions.evidence_quote: This is most evident for the configuration based on the GraphRAG default prompt, i.e., GRdef , which has the lowest rejection rate for GPT-4o-mini, 12.66%, which demonstrates the model’s propensity to be overconfident. Despite some variation across configurations, rejection rates are quite low (all below 50%), indicating the overall challenge faced by current RAG systems in effectively rejecting unanswerable questions.
